skos:definition.@value: Member of Youth Parliament: a young person aged 11 to 18, elected to represent their area in the UK Youth Parliament.
The UK's largest youth ballot, which chooses the issues the UK Youth Parliament debates.

Lowering the voting age to 16 for UK general elections. 16 and 17 year olds already vote in Scottish and Welsh parliament and council elections; the Representation of the People Bill is before the House of Lords.
A group of MPs or peers who look into a subject and report. The Youth Select Committee is the young people's version.
Protecting children and young people from harm, and acting when you are worried about someone.
A criminal record check for adults working with young people: DBS in England and Wales, PVG in Scotland and AccessNI in Northern Ireland.
The law requiring online services to protect children, including checking ages for some content. Further rules for under 16s on social media are due to apply from spring 2027.
Ways online services check a user's age, required for some content under the Online Safety Act.
Where a fact came from. On Amplify, V means verified against the source, S means found by search, and K means a lead still to confirm.
A way to prioritise: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time.
Code anyone can read, learn from and suggest changes to. Amplify's code is open on GitHub.
A note on GitHub describing an idea, a bug or a question. Anyone 13 or over with an account can open one.
A proposed change to the code or content. A person reviews it, and automated checks must pass, before it is accepted.
Automated checks that run on every proposed change, so mistakes are caught before they reach the portal.
Building, testing, releasing and running software together, with automation, so changes are small, safe and frequent.
The international accessibility standard Amplify aims to meet, so disabled people can use it.
British Sign Language and Irish Sign Language, both recognised in law in the UK.
An annual week of events about democracy for young people across the UK. Amplify launches during it, 23 to 29 November 2026.
A version that is ready to test but not yet launched.
Designing around the real needs of the people who use a service, found through research and tested with them.
A short portrait of a kind of user, with their goals, needs and pain points. Amplify's are proto-personas until research tests them.
A need written as 'As a ..., I want to ..., so that ...', with what must be true for it to be done.
The steps someone takes to reach a goal, with what they do and feel at each stage.
A map of a service from what users do, through what the page shows and what happens behind it, to the processes and checks that keep it working.
Learning from the people who use a service, through interviews, testing and co-design, to decide what to build.
Ten standard questions that give a usability score from 0 to 100, compared between research rounds. By John Brooke, 1986.

skos:altLabel.@value: business, data, application, technology and security architecture

skos:definition.@value: Designing how an organisation's business, data, applications, technology and security fit together, layer by layer, in line with its strategy.
The profession for digital, data and technology roles across government, described in its capability framework, from trainee levels up.
A paid job with training towards a recognised qualification. Government and the public sector offer them in every nation, many with no degree needed.
Understanding how artificial intelligence works, where it goes wrong (such as bias and privacy) and how to use it responsibly.
The ordered list of everything asked for, each with a priority, a status and links to where it is built and how it is checked.
What is being worked on now, next and later, and why, updated as priorities change.

skos:altLabel.@value: not in education, employment or training
young people out of work and learning

skos:definition.@value: Not in education, employment or training: the official term for 16 to 24 year olds who are not studying, working or training.

The stage where a bill is examined line by line and changes (amendments) are debated. In the House of Lords it is often a Committee of the Whole House, held in the Chamber so every peer can take part.

The agenda for the day in the House of Commons, published every sitting day: the day's business in the Chamber and Westminster Hall, announcements and future business. Short-notice items such as urgent questions are not on it in advance.
The formal start of the parliamentary year, when the King gives a speech in the House of Lords, written by the Government, setting out the laws it plans for the new session.
The Leader of the House of Commons' statement every sitting Thursday announcing next week's business. MPs then question the Leader on it (Business Questions), often asking for debates.
An MP or peer appointed by a party to make sure colleagues vote with the party, organise business and share information. Also the weekly notice telling members how to vote.
An independent member of the House of Lords who belongs to no party and has no whip. Crossbenchers elect a Convenor to keep them informed.
A select committee of MPs that considers how the House of Commons conducts its business and recommends changes to its rules (Standing Orders). The Lords has its own.
A debate held in a second debating room off Westminster Hall, alongside the Commons Chamber. E-petitions recommended by the Petitions Committee are debated here.
A half-hour debate at the end of each Commons sitting day, where one backbench MP raises an issue and the relevant minister replies.
Someone old enough to register to vote but not yet old enough to vote: 14 to 15 in Scotland and Wales, 16 to 17 in England and Northern Ireland.
A free photo ID document for voting, for registered voters who have no other accepted photo ID. A young person's bus pass is not accepted ID.
The ages at which civic and political rights open up, which differ by nation: registering to vote, voting, standing for election, trusteeship, governorship and jury service.
The monarch's approval of a Bill once both Houses have agreed its text. The Bill then becomes an Act of Parliament.
A group of people chosen by civic lottery to reflect the population, who hear evidence and make recommendations. Climate Assembly UK was commissioned by six Commons select committees.
People voting directly on how part of a public budget is spent. In Scotland young people can vote in youth rounds with their Young Scot card.

skos:altLabel.@value: responsible adult at a police station

skos:definition.@value: An adult who must support anyone under 18, or anyone vulnerable, while they are at a police station.
A person on a charity's governing board. In England and Wales the minimum age is 16 for a charitable company or CIO and 18 for other charities.
Living in a household whose income, once rent or mortgage is paid, is below 60% of the middle (median) UK household income. The UK's headline measure of child poverty.
Free school lunches for pupils whose families get certain benefits. How many pupils are eligible is a common measure of disadvantage in schools.
A legal document in England for a child or young person up to 25 with special educational needs who needs more support than a school can usually give. It says what support they must get.
A pupil who is exposed at home to a language other than English. It describes the language at home, not how well the pupil speaks English.
A child in the care of a council, for example living with foster carers or in a children's home. Councils act as their corporate parent.
A child or young person who gives unpaid care to a family member or friend who is ill, disabled, has a mental health condition or misuses drugs or alcohol.
A way of writing that uses short sentences, one idea in each, everyday words and a picture beside each sentence, so more people can understand.
The section of a political party for its younger members, with its own age range and activities. Each party sets its own rules.
People from different local groups, such as schools, faith groups and unions, listening to each other and acting together on shared issues.
Websites and tools that help people find, follow and contact the people who represent them, or take part in decisions.
A counter that adds one to a daily total each time a screen opens. It keeps no cookie, no IP address and nothing that identifies a person or browser.
A setting in some browsers that tells websites not to sell or share your data or track you. Amplify's counter never counts a browser that sends it.
A written check, done before using people's data, of what could go wrong for them and how it is prevented. Services likely to be used by children must do one first.
